title: Stress Testing & Regulatory Scenarios
gist: Oxford Economics' stress-testing service page lays out its methodology (GEM-based scenarios, reverse stress testing, climate risk fully integrated into the macro model rather than bolted on) and reveals via its live content slate that trade-policy uncertainty is easing while Iran/Strait of Hormuz energy risk and tariff-driven supply chain vulnerability remain the active stress-scenario inputs. Client testimonials (CMHC, Cynergy) show multi-year, retained demand for outsourced regulatory scenario infrastructure.

insights.claim: Banks and insurers operating across multiple jurisdictions must satisfy a patchwork of distinct supervisory stress-test regimes simultaneously, including the US Federal Reserve's CCAR and DFAST, the EBA/ECB's SREP, the Bank of England/PRA's Bank Capital Stress Test (BCST), and separate stress tests run by Hong Kong's HKMA, Singapore's MAS, Australia's APRA and Canada's OSFI.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Multinational banks face compounding compliance cost from reconciling capital scenarios across US, EU, UK and Asia-Pacific regulators; investors should watch for consolidation or standardization pressure in this space.
insights.quote:
Federal Reserve CCAR and DFAST 
EBA and ECB SREP 
Bank of England and PRA Bank Capital
Stress Test (BCST) 
HKMA, MAS, APRA and OSFI stress tests

themes.theme: Methodology: reverse stress testing and integrated climate-macro modelling

insights.claim: Reverse stress testing works backward from a defined point of institutional failure to identify which combinations of economic conditions could produce it, rather than forecasting outcomes forward from an assumed shock.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Signals that boards and regulators are pushing beyond standard forward scenario testing toward identifying the specific tail-risk combinations that would break a given institution's balance sheet.
insights.quote: Work back from a defined point of failure to identify the combinations of economic conditions that could produce it.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics models climate transition and physical risk directly inside the same macroeconomic model used to forecast growth, inflation and financial markets, rather than treating climate as a separate bolt-on overlay to conventional stress scenarios.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Marks a methodological shift from siloed ESG/climate satellite models toward fully endogenous macro-climate integration; useful benchmark when evaluating whether a bank's internal climate stress model is genuinely integrated or just an add-on.
insights.quote: By integrating climate risk within the same framework that models growth, inflation and financial market outcomes, rather than treating it as a separate overlay, we provide a consistent evidence base for climate stress testing, regulatory disclosure and resilience planning.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' climate scenario coverage runs to 2060 across 59 economies, with subnational physical- and transition-risk forecasts for nearly 3,000 cities and regions across the UK, Europe, US and Canada, built on both NGFS-aligned and proprietary scenario pathways.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Shows the city-level granularity now expected in credible climate risk disclosure and stress testing, raising the bar for what counts as adequate climate risk analysis under emerging regulatory disclosure regimes.
insights.quote: Short- and long-term scenarios to 2060 across 59 economies

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' Global Economic Model covers 200+ countries, 100 industries and 8,000 cities and regions within one internally consistent framework, backed by more than 400 in-house economists who can be challenged directly on scenario assumptions.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: This breadth-plus-consistency combination is the basis of the firm's moat versus boutique scenario providers or banks' in-house economics teams, relevant when assessing scenario-data vendors as investable or as counterparties.
insights.quote: We cover 200+ countries, 100 industries and 8,000 cities and regions within one consistent framework, showing how shocks affect the geographies and sectors that matter most.
insights.locator: Macro, global-to-city and industry coverage in one consistent model

themes.theme: Client validation of outsourced stress-testing demand

insights.claim: Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation's Stress-Testing and ORSA team began using Oxford Economics for stress testing and scenario design, praising the software's ability to show the links between variables and its degree of customization, indicating even a government-backed mortgage insurer is professionalizing and outsourcing its ORSA infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Points to demand growth for third-party stress-testing infrastructure extending beyond banks into mortgage insurers and housing-finance agencies.
insights.quote: The software is sound, intuitive and user friendly. But most of all, it allows the user to understand the links between the variables and for a certain degree of customization.

insights.claim: UK financial institution Cynergy has used Oxford Economics for several years to support its modelling and stress testing, describing the output as instrumental in shaping its strategic decision-making, indicating multi-year retained usage rather than a one-off engagement.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Multi-year client retention suggests a sticky, recurring-revenue engagement model for third-party scenario providers in this niche.
insights.quote: We have used Oxford Economics to support our modelling and stress testing for the last few years, and they have consistently delivered high-quality, data-driven insights that have been instrumental in shaping our strategic decision-making.

themes.theme: Current risk themes: trade policy and Middle East energy risk

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' concurrent research frames trade policy as the dominant near-term macro risk swing factor, describing a 'risk pendulum' moving from the inflation fight to trade tensions, and reporting that sentiment in its IFRS 9/CECL expected-credit-loss scenarios has improved as trade policy uncertainty eases.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Credit-risk modelers should check whether bank provisioning baselines have followed this same shift toward more favorable expected-credit-loss assumptions as tariff uncertainty recedes.
insights.quote: Risk pendulum swings from inflation fight to trade tensions, economy to gradually gain momentum.

insights.claim: Alongside easing trade-policy uncertainty, Oxford Economics is separately tracking Iran and the Strait of Hormuz as a live risk to global energy prices, while also producing dedicated tariff-risk and supply-chain-vulnerability mapping for Ontario municipalities and for Asia, indicating trade policy and Middle East energy-supply disruption are the two tail risks currently embedded in client stress scenarios.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Investors modeling energy-price or supply-chain shock scenarios should note these are the specific inputs Oxford Economics' financial-institution clients are currently being asked to stress-test against.
insights.quote: Iran and the Strait of Hormuz: risks to global energy prices
